question: Even very ticklish people cannot tickle themselves, no matter how hard they try. What is it about the brain that makes self-tickling fail?
correct_answer: Brain predicts and cancels self-made touch
alternative_answers: The brain knows the touch is coming
Expected touch is dampened by the brain
You know where and when the touch will land
headline_answer: Brain predicts and cancels self-made touch
source_excerpt: The more participants attenuate the perception of their self-generated touch, the stronger the functional connectivity between the cerebellum and the somatosensory cortical areas

extra.verification_notes: Cerebellar forward-model prediction attenuating self-generated touch is the standard explanation (Blakemore et al.; PMC6975290).

explanation: When you move your own hand, the brain sends a copy of the motor command to the cerebellum, which forecasts the sensation that touch will produce. Because the prediction matches what arrives, the sensory signal is dampened before it reaches full awareness. Tickling relies on unpredictability, so a touch the brain already expected feels dull. When another person tickles you, there is no motor command to predict from, so the sensation arrives at full strength. Studies by Blakemore, Wolpert and Frith in 1998 even showed that a robot arm introducing a small random delay made self-tickling work again.

question: The smallest bone in the human body is about the size of a grain of rice. In which part of the body is it found?
source_excerpt: The stapes is the smallest and lightest bone in the human body

extra.why_interesting: Players picture bones as structural supports in limbs and fingers; the smallest one lives somewhere they never think of as having bones at all.
extra.verification_notes: The stapes in the middle ear is the smallest bone in the human body, per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stapes; I found no newer developments that change this.

explanation: It is the stapes, or stirrup bone, deep in the middle ear, barely 3 millimetres long. Together with two neighbours it passes vibrations from the eardrum inward.

question: A giraffe's neck is about two metres long, yet it contains exactly the same number of vertebrae as your own neck. How many is that?
source_excerpt: Giraffes have seven neck vertebrae – the same number of neck bones that humans have.

extra.why_interesting: The player assumes a two-metre giraffe neck must contain far more bones than a human neck; it contains exactly the same number.
extra.verification_notes: Giraffes and humans both have seven cervical vertebrae; the roughly 2 m neck length is also accurate (https://www.snopes.com/fact-check/giraffes-neck-bones-humans/).

explanation: Nearly every mammal, from a mouse to a giraffe, has seven neck vertebrae. The giraffe simply stretches each one to around 25 centimetres.

question: Every bone in the human skeleton connects to at least one other bone, with a single exception that floats in the throat, held only by muscles. Which bone is it?
source_excerpt: It is the only bone in the human body that is not connected to any other bones.

extra.why_interesting: A skeleton is imagined as one connected frame; one bone floats free, anchored only by soft tissue, and it is essential for speech and swallowing.
extra.verification_notes: The hyoid is widely recognised as the only bone that does not articulate with another bone; 'only by muscles' is a slight simplification since ligaments also anchor it.

explanation: The horseshoe-shaped hyoid sits above the voice box, anchoring the tongue and larynx. Its free-floating position is why forensic examiners check it for fractures in suspected strangulation.

question: Surgeons can remove up to two-thirds of this human organ and it will regrow to roughly its full size within months. Which organ?
source_excerpt: Only 10% of the original liver mass is required for the organ to regenerate back to full size.

extra.why_interesting: Humans are assumed to be poor at regrowing anything; one major organ can rebuild most of itself, which is what makes living-donor transplants possible.
extra.verification_notes: The liver regenerates to roughly full size after resection of up to two-thirds, per Wikipedia's liver regeneration article; no newer development contradicts this.

explanation: This regrowth is what allows a living donor to give part of their liver to a patient, after which both portions grow back. The ancient Greeks may have known it too: Prometheus's punishment was an eagle eating his liver, which regrew each night.

question: One part of the human eye contains no blood vessels at all and absorbs its oxygen directly from the air. Which part?
source_excerpt: the healthy cornea does not have or need blood vessels within it.

extra.why_interesting: Every living tissue is assumed to be fed by blood; one transparent tissue has no blood supply at all, because blood vessels would block the view.
extra.verification_notes: The cornea is avascular and receives oxygen dissolved from the tear film/air; the lens is also avascular but is nourished by aqueous humor, so the answer is unambiguous (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornea).

explanation: Blood vessels would cloud the clear front window of the eye, so the cornea breathes through the tear film instead. That is also why wearing contact lenses too long can starve it of oxygen.

question: Your right lung has three lobes, but your left lung has only two and is noticeably smaller. Which organ is the reason it had to make room?
source_excerpt: The left lung shares space with the heart, and has an indentation in its border called the cardiac notch of the left lung to accommodate this.

extra.why_interesting: Players assume the body is symmetrical; the lungs are not, and the reason is a neighbour they know well once they think about it.
extra.verification_notes: Wikipedia confirms the left lung has two lobes, is smaller than the right, and has a cardiac notch to accommodate the heart.

explanation: The heart sits slightly left of centre, with a notch in the left lung carved out to fit around it. The right lung compensates by being larger and heavier.

question: In 1980 the World Health Organization declared a disease eradicated worldwide, the only human disease ever wiped out completely. Which disease?
source_excerpt: Two infectious diseases have successfully been eradicated: smallpox in humans, and rinderpest in ruminants.

extra.why_interesting: Medicine has defeated many diseases in the public imagination, yet exactly one human disease has actually been wiped from the planet.
extra.verification_notes: Smallpox was declared eradicated by WHO in 1980 and remains the only eradicated human disease as of 2026 (rinderpest is animal-only; guinea worm and polio not yet eradicated), per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eradication_of_infectious_diseases.

explanation: The last natural case was recorded in Somalia in 1977 after a global vaccination campaign. Only two laboratories, in the United States and Russia, still hold samples of the virus.

question: The painkiller aspirin was developed from a compound found in the bark of which tree, chewed for pain relief since ancient Greece?
source_excerpt: A precursor compound called salicin, found in willow tree bark, is metabolized into salicylic acid and has been used for its health effects for at least 2,400 years.

extra.why_interesting: Aspirin feels like a purely synthetic laboratory product, yet its chemistry comes from a tree that Hippocrates was already prescribing.
extra.verification_notes: Aspirin derives from salicin found in willow (Salix) bark, used medicinally since classical antiquity per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aspirin; the 'chewed' detail is loose but not wrong.

explanation: Willow bark contains salicin, which chemists at Bayer turned into acetylsalicylic acid in the 1890s. Hippocrates recommended willow leaf tea for pain more than two thousand years earlier.

question: Which metal, bound inside the haemoglobin of your red blood cells, carries oxygen and gives human blood its red colour?
source_excerpt: A heme group consists of an iron (Fe) ion held in a heterocyclic ring, known as a porphyrin.

extra.why_interesting: The player knows blood is red and that anaemia involves a metal, but may not connect the two; the metal in their blood is the same one that rusts red.
extra.verification_notes: Heme iron in haemoglobin binds oxygen and is the only metal involved; the colour nuance (porphyrin ring) doesn't create another defensible answer (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hemoglobin).

explanation: An adult body holds roughly four grams of iron, most of it in the blood. Horseshoe crabs use copper instead, which is why their blood is blue.

question: True or false: an adult is measurably taller when they wake up in the morning than when they go to bed at night.
source_excerpt: Quantitative Assessment of Intervertebral Disc Composition by MRI: Sensitivity to Diurnal Variation

extra.why_interesting: Height feels like a fixed number; in reality it changes measurably every single day, and the player's own spine is the mechanism.
extra.verification_notes: Well-established diurnal height variation of roughly 0.6–2 cm from spinal disc compression and rehydration; no newer findings contradict it (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC10204382/).

explanation: True. The cushioning discs between your vertebrae compress by one to two centimetres over a day of standing and sitting, then re-expand while you lie down overnight.

question: Before this breakthrough in Toronto, a child diagnosed with type 1 diabetes rarely survived more than a couple of years. In which year was insulin first injected into a human patient?
source_excerpt: At Toronto General Hospital on 11 January 1922, house physician Ed Jeffrey injected Leonard Thompson with a beef-pancreas extract prepared by Frederick Banting and Charles Best.

extra.why_interesting: Diabetes is ancient and insulin feels like old medicine, yet before the 1920s a childhood diagnosis of type 1 diabetes was a death sentence within a year or two.
extra.verification_notes: Leonard Thompson received the first human insulin injection on 11 January 1922 at Toronto General Hospital (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Thompson_(diabetic)).

explanation: Fourteen-year-old Leonard Thompson received the first injection in January 1922, after Frederick Banting and Charles Best isolated insulin the previous year. Banting shared a Nobel Prize for it just one year later, in 1923.

question: A resting heart beats around 70 times a minute. Over an 80-year lifetime, roughly how many times does a human heart beat?
source_excerpt: How Many Times Does Your Heart Beat in a Lifetime? (2.5 Billion — Exact Math)

extra.why_interesting: The player can estimate from a familiar pulse rate but tends to stop a factor of ten short; the true lifetime total lands in the billions.
extra.verification_notes: 70 bpm × 80 years ≈ 2.94 billion beats, so 'Billions' is correct; sources cite ~2.5–3 billion (https://easetoolz.com/blog/heartbeat-in-a-lifetime).

explanation: Seventy beats a minute adds up to about 100,000 a day, 37 million a year, and close to 3 billion over 80 years. The heart does all of that without ever taking a day off.

question: Which organ in the human digestive system, despite its name, stretches to around six metres in length?
source_excerpt: The small intestine is about 6.5 metres (21 feet) long and folds many times to fit in the abdomen.

extra.why_interesting: Players hear 'small' and assume it is the short one; the answer flips that, and the explanation resolves it by revealing the name describes width, not length.
extra.verification_notes: Small intestine is commonly cited as ~6 m (6.5 m in cadavers, shorter in living people), and no other digestive organ with a misleading name approaches this length; source https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Small_intestine

explanation: The small intestine is about four times longer than the large intestine; it is called small because it is narrower, not shorter.
